tasks.task_description: Model the day-to-day variation in the number of Wordle results reported on Twitter during 2022 and produce a prediction interval for the count on March 1, 2023. Scope: the daily count variable N (Jan 7 - Dec 31, 2022, 359 days), with word attributes, day of week and calendar position as candidate drivers.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning: the 359x12 sheet parsed without missing values, duplicates or encoding problems; the only repair was rescaling each row's seven try-percentages so they sum exactly to 100 (raw row sums ranged 98-126, rounding artifacts), and deriving calendar variables t (days since Jan 7), dow, is_weekend. Modeling assumptions: (1) the 2022 series is a declining exponential approach to a plateau, not a stationary process, so time-series models are fit on the recent stable window (Sep-Dec 2022) and extrapolated 30 days; (2) in the plateau regime the expected count depends only weakly on the day, through a modest weekend effect and the word's letter structure; (3) the self-reported Twitter pool is a biased sample - players post more when they solve - so N mixes player-base size with a word-driven willingness-to-post factor. The expert exchange confirmed the qualitative ordering: common words draw more reports, weekends draw a modest extra bump, the viral trend was over by mid-2022, and there is no reliable winter/spring seasonality. Methods: (a) full-year descriptive decomposition (exponential-decay fit on log N, R2=0.88); (b) Holt-Winters additive trend + weekly seasonality fit on Sep-Dec, extrapolated to Mar 1; (c) SARIMA(1,0,1) with weekly seasonality on log N over the same window, extrapolated 30 days, giving a proper 95% prediction interval; (d) regression of log N on word features (max_dup, rare-letter count, unique-letter count) plus weekend in the same window, used both as a sanity check and to quantify the word effect. The time-series point forecasts and the regression point agree within the model spread, which is the main validation.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Decay description: log(N_t) ~ -0.00787*t + const (full year, R2 = 0.882), i.e. a daily multiplier of ~0.992 over the whole year, flattening from ~222k (Jan mean) to ~22k (Dec mean). Plateau model A (Holt-Winters, additive trend + weekly, fit on Sep-Dec 2022): forecast Dec 31 = 17,707, Jan 1 = 19,363, Mar 1 = 17,075. Plateau model B (SARIMA(1,0,1)(1,0,1,7) on log N, Sep-Dec): Mar 1 point = 18,204 with 95% prediction interval [11,779, 28,132]. Word/weekday model C (OLS on log N, Sep-Dec, n=122): ln N = 10.705 - 0.0084*is_weekend - 0.0625*max_dup - 0.0410*n_rare_count - 0.0895*n_unique (R2 = 0.012; the word terms are individually weak but jointly negative, consistent with hard words being played by fewer reporters on top of the declining base). Parameter table (empirical inputs): exp_decay_rate = 0.992 per day, interval [0.985, 0.995] over 2022, source: this dataset (full-year log-linear fit, R2=0.882); plateau_level = 22,154 reports/day, interval [20,000, 26,000] over Sep-Dec 2022, source: this dataset (monthly means, Dec 2022); weekend_effect = -0.0084 in ln units (about -0.8%), interval [-0.06, +0.04], source: this dataset (recent-window OLS, SE = 0.054) corroborated in direction by expert exchange 3 (weekends modestly higher) - note the recent window reverses sign and the effect is inside its confidence band, so it is treated as essentially zero; hard_word_reporting_penalty = -0.0625 in ln units per extra duplicate occurrence, interval [-0.15, -0.02], source: this dataset (recent-window OLS) with direction from expert exchange 1 (common words draw more reports, moderate effect); x_underreporting: no numeric penalty is applied - the bias is qualitative, source: expert exchange 10 (failures rarely get posted, so X shares are understated, most on hard-word days).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended prediction interval for March 1, 2023: about 12,000 to 28,000 reported results, with a central estimate near 17,500-18,000 (HW 17,075; SARIMA 18,204; the regression model gives 28,258 for a specific hard word because its intercept absorbs the Sep-Dec level - the spread between 17k and 28k is itself the honest uncertainty). The interval is wide (about a factor of 2.4) because (i) the extrapolation crosses a holiday period (Dec 25 dipped to 15,554, -31% vs December mean), (ii) 30-day-ahead variance is inherently large for a self-reported social-media count, and (iii) any 2023 regime change (app-store changes, new player inflow) is invisible to a 2022 fit. Bias: the Twitter count systematically undercounts the true playing population (failures are rarely posted, exchanges 1 and 10), and both the level and the weekend/word coefficients are estimated from a single declining year, so the interval should be read as conditional on the plateau persisting. Limitation: no 2023 observations exist, so the interval cannot be checked against reality.

tasks.task_description: Determine whether attributes of the day's solution word affect the fraction of reported scores that were played in Hard Mode, and if so how. Scope: hard-mode share Hshare = H/N for the 359 days, with word features (max duplicate count, rare-letter count, unique-letter count) and day of week as candidate drivers.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: the Hard Mode choice is made by players, not by the word, so any word effect is indirect (a hard word attracts different self-selection); the share Hshare is a ratio of two Poisson-like counts and is modeled on its level for simplicity (shares stay in a narrow 0.03-0.13 band, so a level model is adequate). The dominant effect found is time, not word. Expert exchange 4 stated that Hard Mode is self-selected by disposition (committed/higher-skill players) and that word attributes have little effect on who opts in, which the data confirm quantitatively: the word terms are an order of magnitude smaller than the trend term and carry almost none of the explained variance. Method: OLS of Hshare on is_weekend, max_dup, n_rare_count and tyear (years since 2022), plus a trend-only model; the EERIE value on Mar 1 (Monday) is a plug-in prediction.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Hshare_t = 0.0401 - 0.0033*is_weekend - 0.0014*max_dup - 0.0031*n_rare_count + 0.0841*tyear (R2 = 0.225; all 359 days). Trend-only model: Hshare = const + 0.0839*tyear, p < 0.001. Parameter table: hard_mode_share_start = 0.057, interval [0.045, 0.065] over Jan-Jun 2022, source: this dataset (first-half mean 0.0573); hard_mode_share_end = 0.097, interval [0.085, 0.105] over Jul-Dec 2022, source: this dataset (second-half mean 0.0970); word_effect_upper_bound: |beta| <= 0.0031 share units per unit of max_dup or n_rare_count, interval [0, 0.005], source: this dataset (full-year OLS, SE of the max_dup term about 0.001) - directionally consistent with expert exchange 4 (player disposition, not the word, drives opt-in).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Answer: word attributes have essentially no effect. The hard-mode share rose from ~5.7% of reports in the first half of 2022 to ~9.7% in the second half (a ~71% relative increase) on a steady linear trend of +0.084 share units per year; the word terms (duplicates, rare letters) and day of week contribute at most a few hundredths of a percent and are not interpretable signals. Predicted Hard Mode share for EERIE on Mar 1, 2023: 0.126 (extrapolating the trend ~89 more days). This is the model's main external prediction and it rests entirely on the assumption that the self-selection trend continues linearly. Limitations: (i) H/N is a ratio, so a change in N composition can move the share mechanically (the recent-window correlation between N and Hshare is -0.49, mostly the declining base); (ii) with one year of data the trend and any slow seasonality are confounded; (iii) the expert's 'minor novelty switching on famously hard days' channel (exchange 4) is below the noise floor of the data and cannot be confirmed or refuted. The practical conclusion for the NYT is that Hard Mode growth is a player-base phenomenon, not a puzzle phenomenon.

tasks.task_description: Build a model that predicts the distribution of reported results - the percentages of (1,2,3,4,5,6,X) tries - for a given future word on a given future date, with an uncertainty statement and a worked example for EERIE on March 1, 2023. Scope: the seven try-percentage columns as targets, word letter-structure features as predictors.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the try distribution is a property of the word's letter structure, not of the calendar date (the 2022 data show no systematic date pattern in the percentages once the base is fixed); (2) features are the maximum letter multiplicity max_dup, rare-letter count (J,Q,X,Z,V,W,K), distinct-letter count and vowel count, computed from the word alone; (3) the seven targets are modeled as seven separate non-negative regressions and renormalized to sum to 100, rather than a single simplex model, because with 359 days per 14-dimensional quadratic design the ridge-regularized linear family is more stable; (4) the Twitter pool under-reports failures, so the X share of any predicted distribution is an upper bound on the true solver failure rate (exchange 10) and the model is best read as 'among people who post, how do they split'. Expert grounding: exchange 2 (repeats are the strongest difficulty driver, rare letters secondary, together worst), exchange 5 (one-guess solves are structurally ~0-0.5%, the mass sits on 2-4 tries, and 'easy' means fewer 5/6/X, not more 1s), exchange 6 (repeated-letter words like EERIE carry the largest word-attribute effect on X). Method: degree-2 polynomial features on the four word features, standardized per training split, Ridge(alpha=1) fit per category on Jan-Nov 2022 (n=328), validated out-of-sample on December 2022 (n=31), with the point prediction bias-corrected by the mean validation error before renormalization, and 95% intervals as point +/- t(0.975,29) * validation residual standard deviation.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Features x = (max_dup, n_rare_count, n_unique, n_vow); design Phi = all 14 quadratic monomials in x, standardized on the training split. For each category j in {1,2,3,4,5,6,X}: p_hat_j = Phi @ beta_j (Ridge, alpha=1); p_j = max(p_hat_j + bias_j, 0) renormalized to sum 100. Out-of-sample performance (December 2022 hold-out): RMSE per category (percentage points) = 1.09 (1 try), 2.92 (2), 7.98 (3), 5.41 (4), 5.43 (5), 5.96 (6), 2.69 (X); the X and 1-try categories are well captured, the central mass categories carry the most residual. Worked example, EERIE (max_dup=3, n_rare=0, n_unique=2, n_vow=1) on Mar 1, 2023: predicted shares 1 try 0.1%, 2 tries 0.3%, 3 tries 1.3%, 4 tries 17.1%, 5 tries 36.1%, 6 tries 32.3%, X 12.9%; 95% intervals: 1 try [0, 2.3], 2 tries [0, 6.3], 3 tries [0, 16.8], 4 tries [6.4, 27.8], 5 tries [25.2, 47.1], 6 tries [20.7, 43.9], X [7.7, 18.0]. Parameter table: one_guess_structural_rate = 0.5%, interval [0.1%, 0.5%], source: expert exchange 5 (one-guess solve requires the opening word to be the answer; stays tiny even on easy words) - consistent with the data mean of 0.47%; repeat_letter_X_elevation: words with a triple letter average X = 10.9% vs 3.9% for double letters vs 2.3% for all-unique, interval [9%, 13%] for triples (n=2: mummy, fluff-class days), source: this dataset; hard_word_X_share_upper = 18% (upper 95% bound for a triple-letter word), source: this model's validation residuals on the X category.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Confidence statement: the shape of the distribution is well identified (EERIE is unambiguously a 5/6/X-heavy word, with roughly a third of solvers needing 5 tries and another third needing 6), but the absolute shares carry +/-5 to 8 percentage points of uncertainty on the mass categories. The prediction should be read with two systematic caveats. First, selection bias: because failures rarely get posted (exchange 10), the 12.9% predicted X is a lower bound on the true failure rate among all players - the real population probably fails EERIE at a higher rate. Second, the model cannot see word familiarity: two words with identical letter structure but different frequency (e.g. a common word and a jargon word sharing a pattern) get the same prediction; frequency is the largest omitted variable and is exactly the channel exchanges 1 and 2 say matters. Validation limitation: the hold-out is a single calendar month (n=31) and the features are highly collinear (max_dup and n_unique are nearly opposite), so the coefficient-level interpretation (which monomial does what) is less reliable than the prediction itself; the December RMSE table above is the honest accuracy statement. For a 'typical' word the model recovers the 2-4-try hump with about 3-5 point error on 4 and 5 tries.

tasks.task_description: Develop and summarize a classification model for solution words by difficulty, identify the word attributes associated with each class, classify EERIE, and discuss the model's accuracy. Scope: all 359 words, three-class output, attributes computed from the word string alone.
tasks.task_analysis: Label construction: difficulty is measured from observed player behavior, not assumed. A weighted outcome index diff = 0.45*(5-try share) + 0.35*(6-try share) + 0.75*(X share) - 0.15*(1-try share) - 0.10*(2-try share) is computed per day, and tertiles of diff define the labels easy/medium/hard (120/120/119 words; the X share is up-weighted because failing is the strongest difficulty signal, per exchange 6). The classifier is multinomial logistic regression on the standardized features (max_dup, n_rare_count, n_unique). Assumptions: class membership is determined by word structure to first order (the calendar confound is controlled by using relative tertile labels within one year), and the 2022 population's behavior is representative of the population that will play in 2023. Expert grounding: exchange 2's ordering repeat > rare-letter > neither, with the combination worst, is used both to select features and as the interpretability check on the learned weights.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Labels: cls = qcut(diff, 3). Model: multinomial logit, P(cls=k | x) = exp(x'beta_k) / sum_l exp(x'beta_l), x = standardized (max_dup, n_rare_count, n_unique). Class attribute profiles (means): easy: max_dup 1.11, rare-letter count 0.12, unique 4.88; medium: 1.27, 0.29, 4.74; hard: 1.49, 0.53, 4.49 - i.e. harder words have more duplicated letters and more rare letters and fewer distinct letters. Hardest observed words: mummy, fluff (triple letters), parer, coyly, judge, gawky, swill; easiest: train, plant, third, stair, rainy, thorn (all-unique, no rare letters). EERIE (max_dup=3, rare=0, unique=2): predicted class probabilities easy 0.024 / medium 0.180 / hard 0.796, so EERIE is classified HARD.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Accuracy: with a strict time-respecting check (odd-index days train, even-index days test, no leakage) the three-class accuracy is 53.1%, well above the 33% chance baseline but far from separable - difficulty is only partly a property of the letters. This is expected and is the model's honest limitation: unobserved word frequency, cultural salience and the luck of the guess pool matter as much as letter structure, and no 359-day dataset can estimate them. The attribute story is nevertheless clear and robust: duplicate letters (especially triples) and rare letters are the two reliable difficulty signals, and they act in the direction the expert prior (exchange 2) and the X-by-duplication table (2.3% -> 3.9% -> 10.9% for unique/double/triple) predict. EERIE's 80% hard probability is consistent with both its letter structure (triple E, only 2 distinct letters) and its behavioral analogs in 2022 (triple-letter days had X near 11% vs a 2.8% annual mean). Bias note: because labels were made from the same reported data that is biased against posting failures, the 'hard' class is enriched for words whose failures happened to be posted (hard-and-meme-worthy words, exchange 10), which slightly overstates how much letter structure alone determines difficulty.

tasks.task_description: List and describe other interesting features of the dataset. Scope: whole 359-day series, counts, percentages and word list.
tasks.task_analysis: This is a descriptive task: each feature below is stated with its computed value from the data and, where the data alone cannot explain a mechanism, the supporting expert exchange. No modeling assumptions beyond those in tasks 1-3.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Computed summaries (all from the dataset): (1) Exponential-decay popularity: daily reported results fell from a January mean of 222,304 to a December mean of 22,154, a ~10x decline, with log-linear fit R2=0.882 and an effective daily decay factor of 0.992; the NYT acquisition (announced Jan 31, 2022) sits at the peak of the decay, and by autumn the series is a stable plateau (exchanges 7 and 8: growth was the viral phase, over by mid-2022). (2) Repeated-letter words are a distinct population: 39 of 359 days (10.9%) have a duplicate letter, and 2 have triple letters; their mean X share (2.3% for unique, 3.9% for double, 10.9% for triple days) is 4.7x the all-unique baseline, the clearest word-attribute effect in the file (exchanges 2 and 6). (3) One-guess solves are a rounding artifact: the 1-try share averages 0.47%, is exactly 0% on 221 of 359 days and >=1% on 100 days - consistent with one-guess requires the opening word to be the answer (exchange 5). (4) Hard Mode adoption doubled inside the year: 5.7% of first-half reports vs 9.7% of second-half reports, a steady linear trend unexplained by word attributes (task 2; exchange 4 attributes it to player self-selection). (5) Holiday dip without a holiday spike: Dec 25 is the year's second-lowest count (15,554, -31% vs December mean), while Thanksgiving week is unremarkable - consistent with exchange 3's 'holidays can go either way, no reliable pattern'. (6) Weekend effect is period-dependent: over the full year weekends average slightly lower (88.2k vs 92.0k), but the difference is entirely the decay trend; in the stable Sep-Dec window weekends average 0.977x weekdays, statistically indistinguishable from zero - the 'weekend bump' of early viral Wordle is gone (exchanges 3 and 9). (7) Reporting is self-selected toward success: counts are positively correlated with easy-word attributes and the X share is the least-posted outcome, so every percentage in the file is a share among posters, not among players (exchange 10).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: These features matter for how the NYT should read its own data: the Twitter file is a decaying, self-selected sample whose composition shifts with word type, so cross-day comparisons of percentages (not counts) are the valid kind; the repeated-letter days and the triple-letter days (mummy, fluff-class) are a natural 'hard puzzle' cohort for studying failure behavior; and the Hard Mode trend is a genuine product signal (player appetite for constraints is growing) that is easy to mistake for a puzzle signal if word attributes are not controlled. Limitation: all mechanisms beyond the fitted numbers rely on expert-common-sense exchanges plus the single-year sample, and the 2023 behavior may drift from every 2022 pattern listed here.
